1:
What Jephthah's mother was is the first question. Ellicott holds that harlot is the only possible rendering, since all the versions give it and a word for an inferior wife was available and unused; he allows only that it may be the harsh word of Jephthah's brothers rather than a strictly accurate one. Clarke would render it hostess, the keeper of an inn for travellers, citing the Targum, which calls her a woman who kept a tavern. He thinks her very probably a Canaanite, since the next verse calls her a woman of another race, and finds there the real reason he was driven out, his mother being no Israelite and his claim on the inheritance imperfect. Henry reports the same guesses without settling them, Josephus making him a stranger on the mother's side and the Jews an Ishmaelite, and adds the point that matters to him: no man ought to be reproached with the infelicities of his parentage while he is labouring by his own merits to roll the reproach away.

The father's name raises a second question. Keil and Delitzsch insist that Gilead is a real man, not the country personified nor the grandson of Manasseh borrowed for an unknown father; the name of a famous ancestor was simply repeated in a descendant, as with the judges named just before. Ellicott leaves it open, the answer depending on a chronology he calls insoluble, but observes that no other Gilead is named, so the grandson of Manasseh is the natural inference, and that an obscure genealogy in Chronicles suggests the house of Manasseh had Aramean connections — in which case Jephthah's mother may have come from the very district he afterwards fled to. On the expulsion itself Ellicott finds no illegality, since it agreed with the law and with old family practice, Abraham having sent away the sons of Hagar and Keturah to settle elsewhere. Henry sees the rigour and not the legality: the legitimate sons stood on the letter of the law and made no allowance for qualities that deserved a dispensation. He notes the double edge of the statute, which shut the Ammonites out of the congregation in the same breath as the base-born, and thinks Jephthah escaped it, the law most probably meaning only those born of incest.

Where he went and what he did there divides them again. Keil and Delitzsch place Tob on the Syrian border north-east of Perea and describe the men who gathered to him going out on warlike and predatory expeditions, after the manner of Bedouins. Ellicott is blunter, calling him a sort of Syrian freebooter, and thinks his half-heathen origin worked on his character as unfavourably as on Abimelech's; the name Tob means good, he adds, but gives no warrant for the idle allegories built on it. Clarke reads the word for his followers as empty men, wanting sense and loose in their manners, though he allows it may mean only men without property, and notes that the versions generally take them for plunderers. Gill and Henry both defend him. Gill has him leave because a man of spirit could not bear contempt nor live in dependence on others; Henry says such a man would neither dig nor beg, so he lived by his sword, the men who joined him were such as had run through their estates, and they went out not to rob but to hunt wild beasts, and perhaps to raid land Israel had a title to and had never yet possessed. Henry draws the moral. Nobody would have picked this outcast for a deliverer, but God often humbles those he means to exalt and makes the stone the builders refused the head of the corner, as with Joseph and Moses and David; and a people who had made themselves children of whoredoms were fitly saved by a bastard and an exile.
4:
The phrase that opens the section is vague on purpose. Keil and Delitzsch take it for a long period that cannot be more precisely defined, and note that the war already reported some chapters back is here resumed so that its course under Jephthah may be told at length. Ellicott measures the interval by the man, from his expulsion in early youth to his mature manhood, and finds the repetition itself significant: that the invasion is introduced as though it were news probably means the writer had turned to a new source for these two chapters, most likely a Gileadite one. Henry notices the reversal in the timing. Many days after Jephthah had been thrust out in disgrace he was fetched back again with honour. He observes too that the elders neither wrote nor sent a messenger but came in person, meaning to take no denial, since the emergency allowed no delay. Ellicott explains why they wanted this man in particular: by now he had a great name as a brave and successful captain of marauders, and his men would come with him.

What they offered him was less than what he took. Ellicott and Keil both note that their word means a leader in war only, and that Jephthah holds out for the other word, a head in peace as well. Gill reads their caution in the offer. They did not propose to make him king, Abimelech having taught them what that came to, and they said nothing of his being judge, since they looked no further than the present emergency, and a judge in any case was not chosen by the people but raised up by God — an honour that came to Jephthah later. Clarke recalls that the command had already been offered to anyone who would take it. Henry draws his conclusion from their helplessness: they knew of no man among themselves equal to the trust and in effect confessed as much, for an army without a general is a body without a head. He turns it into an argument for government at large, since men hearty in a cause still cannot fight without a captain, and every society needs some to rule and others to obey.

Jephthah's first word to them is a reproach. Keil and Delitzsch observe that he lays his expulsion at the door of the elders although only his brothers drove him out, since the elders had either approved it or had failed as magistrates to prevent it; they add that this does not prove the expulsion illegal, only that Jephthah regarded it so. Ellicott agrees they must at least have permitted it, and reads their answer as an express offer to repair the old wrong, which Clarke takes at face value as a confession of injustice. Henry presses the principle harder: magistrates who have power to protect the injured and neglect to redress their grievances are really guilty of inflicting them. He does not think Jephthah unwilling to serve, only careful to remind them of their unkindness so that they might repent of it, as Joseph humbled his brothers before making himself known. The parallel Henry finds most striking is with the nation itself, which had thrust God out by its idolatries and now begged his help in distress, and was told how justly it might have been rejected before it was graciously delivered. From the story he draws two lessons: never to trample on a man because he is mean, since it is wisdom to make no man an enemy when we cannot know whose help we shall need; and for men of worth who are slighted, to bear it quietly and leave it to God to bring their light out of obscurity.
9:
Jephthah drives a bargain before he takes the command. Gill sees the reason in his history, since a man used as he had been, and knowing how fickle men are once their turn is served, would want the terms settled beforehand. Keil and Delitzsch resist reading his words as a question at all: the pronoun is emphatic, and the elders' reply, according to thy words, presupposes a statement rather than an enquiry. Ellicott will not defend the transaction as patriotism. Jephthah was only half an Israelite, had been wronged by his father's kin, and had spent the years of his manhood among heathens and outlaws who lived by brigandage or by hiring out their swords; and Ellicott quotes the judgment that where Gideon is the highest pitch this period reaches, Jephthah and Samson are the lowest points to which it descends. He asks for allowance rather than approval, since if ferocity and religious ignorance mark even the noble character of Gideon, less may be expected of a man so unfavourably placed, the pastoral tribes east of Jordan standing altogether below the farming tribes on the west.

The oath that closes the bargain is read carefully. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both prefer be hearing to be witness, so that the sense is that Jehovah should hear and judge the matter under negotiation; Ellicott cites the Vulgate, which makes him at once the mediator and the witness of it. Clarke follows the three stages by which the appointment was made complete. The elders had chosen him, but the choice needed the people's confirmation, so the people made him head; and even that did not finish the business, since God had to be brought in as a party, which is why Jephthah repeated all his terms before the Lord. Ellicott takes the last act for an oath about the conditions of his government, and notes that the people were inaugurating him as civil and military leader of the tribes beyond Jordan at once. Whether the phrase implies the ark stood there is the one real question. Keil and Delitzsch deny it flatly, since the war was resolved on by the eastern tribes alone and they had no ark; still less will they allow an altar or sacrifices, of which the text gives no hint, and they quote the judgment that the words imply nothing more than that Jephthah confirmed what he said by an oath. Ellicott reports the contrary opinion, that the phrase elsewhere means before the ark or the Urim, and that the scene must therefore be the western Mizpeh in Benjamin. He answers it two ways. Had that Mizpeh been meant it would have been named, since the Mizpeh of this narrative is in Gilead; and the high priest was unlikely to carry the sacred lots into a disturbed and threatened district. Gilead's own Mizpeh, he adds, had sacred associations of its own reaching back to Jacob and Laban.
12:
Jephthah's first act as head is to send an embassy rather than an army. Gill thinks he acted in character, wanting the matter settled amicably, and finds nothing in that inconsistent with a man of valour. Clarke reads a colder motive into it: by making the Ammonites state their own grounds he would let the justice of his cause appear the more forcibly to his people. Keil and Delitzsch note that the ambassadors speak in the name of the nation, which is why the complaint runs in the singular, of my land and against me. Ellicott compares the whole proceeding to the Roman practice of sending heralds ahead of a war to proclaim the justice of the cause. Henry makes most of the delay. It shows that Jephthah did not delight in war, and would not compel by the sword what he could gain by reason; war should be the last remedy, not used until every gentler method has been tried, and he applies the same rule to going to law, since the sword of justice is no more to be appealed to at once than the sword of war. It shows too that Jephthah meant to do justice: had the Ammonites shown him Israel had wronged them, he stood ready to restore their rights.

The answer he gets is a claim of ancient title. Keil and Delitzsch state it plainly — that Israel on coming out of Egypt had taken the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan — and allow it one feature with a certain colour of justice, since part of what Israel held had once been Moabite. Ellicott calls the plea very plausible and not in accordance with the facts. Israel had been expressly forbidden to make war on Moab or Ammon; the land in question was taken from Sihon, who had refused them passage and come out to fight them. That a large district of Sihon's kingdom had originally belonged to Moab and Ammon and been wrested from them by him was quite true, and, says Ellicott, no concern of Israel's; it was absurd to expect a nation to shed its blood for settlements only to hand them back to neighbours who regarded it with the deadliest enmity. He fixes the two rivers as the bounds of Gad and Reuben, the Arnon meaning noisy and cutting Reuben off from Moab by its deep ravine, the Jabbok meaning pouring out and marking Ammon's old border. Clarke adds that the Moabites appear to have been confederate with Ammon in this war.

Henry doubts the claim was ever the real reason. He thinks they came down meaning nothing but plunder, as they had once come under Eglon without raising any such question, and that only when Jephthah demanded their grounds, and they could not for shame own what they had come for, were old musty records searched to furnish a colourable pretence of equity. Even men who do the greatest wrong, he observes, have conscience enough to wish to seem in the right. On the demand to restore the lands he notes on what uncertain terms we hold our worldly possessions, since what we think we hold most surely may be wrested away, while those who have reached the heavenly Canaan need not fear to have their title questioned. He then sets out the defence Jephthah will make. Israel took nothing from Moab or Ammon, whom he treats together as brethren, the children of Lot, close neighbours of united interests with the same god and sometimes the same king; the orders not to meddle with them were religiously observed, and what Israel took, it took from the Amorite. If the Amorites had themselves seized that country from Moab or Ammon beforehand, Israel had no call to enquire into it, and no obligation to win back for another nation what that nation had already lost.
14:
The second embassy answers the claim with a march route. Keil and Delitzsch note that Jephthah proves his case by rehearsing the leading facts of the journey from Egypt, and that his rehearsal agrees exactly with the Pentateuch: Israel came through the desert to the Red Sea and to Kadesh, asked leave of the king of Edom to pass and was refused, asked the same of the king of Moab and was refused again, stayed at Kadesh, and then went round both countries rather than through them. They observe that the embassy to Moab is nowhere recorded in the books of Moses, having had no bearing on the course Israel actually took. Ellicott sees no difficulty in Jephthah's knowing it, since even without documents the events were not so old as to have been forgotten. He glosses the geography as he goes: the Red Sea is in the Hebrew the sea of weeds, Kadesh-barnea was reached from Ezion-geber on the gulf, and the many days spent at Kadesh probably covered a great part of the forty years. Gill adds that they went along the wilderness bordering Edom, passing on the southern side of Edom and Moab.

The war with Sihon is the hinge of the argument. Keil and Delitzsch point out that these verses stand almost word for word as they stand in Numbers, and read the request to pass into my place as meaning into the Canaan that Jehovah had appointed. Ellicott explains the refusal simply: Sihon did not believe the promise to pass through peaceably. Gill supplies the fear behind the disbelief, that Sihon knew his people were of the seven nations whose land Israel was going to take, and expected to lose his own. Ellicott adds that Sihon was king of the Amorites by birth but king of Heshbon only by conquest, the town being afterwards assigned to Reuben, and that the site of the battle at Jahaz has never been identified. Gill makes the same point about Heshbon carry weight in the dispute, since Sihon had taken it from Moab and it was part of the very territory now claimed. Ellicott observes that the conquest of the country east of Jordan had never been part of Israel's plan at all, but was forced on them by the hostility of Sihon and Og. Clarke marks the bounds of what was won, from Arabia Deserta on the east to the Jordan on the west. Gill draws the conclusion Jephthah is working towards: since Sihon and his people and his country fell to Israel by a victory the Lord gave, Israel holds the land by a divine right. Ellicott puts the same thing the other way about, that what Israel took was Sihon's, which they had never been forbidden to take and had indeed been forced to take, and that they could hardly be expected to enter into a discussion about who had owned it before him.
23:
Jephthah now turns the argument on the Ammonite's own religion. Keil and Delitzsch state the first conclusion as simple and indisputable: Jehovah rooted out the Amorites before his people, and shall the claimant take possession of what Jehovah gave? Ellicott puts it as a question of motive: is it likely Israel would fight its battles solely to benefit Ammon and Moab? Clarke sets out the chain: the Ammonites had lost these lands to the Amorites; Israel conquered them from the Amorites, who had made an unprincipled war on them; God granted them to Israel; and the Ammonites never reclaimed them, though they had opportunities enough, because they knew the title was good. Then comes the appeal to Chemosh, which Clarke reads as an argument from a shared maxim. Every nation holds that what its god has given it may keep; you will not give up what you believe Chemosh gave you; we know Jehovah gave us the land of the Amorites, and we will not give that up either. Gill calls it an argument put to the man on his own ground. Ellicott notes what the name betrays, since Chemosh was distinctively the god of Moab and Moloch of Ammon, so the phrase shows how closely the two kindred nations were joined; and he hears a possible echo of the old song of triumph over Heshbon, where Chemosh is taunted by name.

The second argument is from prescription. Keil and Delitzsch see Jephthah adding a further proof to strip the claim of its last appearance of right: is the claimant better than Balak, who never strove or fought with Israel over this land? They note that Balak did hire Balaam against Israel, but from fear rather than any wish to recover Amorite territory. Ellicott takes the comparison as a Hebrew superlative and states its force plainly: even Balak, who hated Israel as deadly as anyone could, never ventured to challenge the title, and by not challenging it admitted it. He meets the apparent conflict with the passage in Joshua where Balak is said to have warred against Israel, answering that it makes no difference to the argument, since Balak fought out of pure hatred and never out of any pretension to their conquests. Gill thinks the comparison strengthens the guess that the man Jephthah addressed ruled Moab as well as Ammon, Balak being one of his predecessors.

The number that closes the argument is the one thing here the commentators cannot agree on. Clarke takes the three hundred years at face value and makes them part of the case, undisturbed possession being the fourth of his five points. Ellicott doubts the phrase belongs to the text at all. He finds an almost insuperable difficulty in fitting it to any chronology, since nine or ten preserved genealogies span the time from the conquest to David in seven or eight generations, and that period includes Samuel's judgeship and Saul's reign; the supposition that generations have been dropped from all of them, even from David's own pedigree, he calls very improbable. He notes besides that the words are needless to Jephthah's argument and actually conflict with the rest of the sentence, which speaks of Balak alone, and suggests they may be a marginal gloss that crept in. If genuine, he thinks they may be counted inclusively, as Jews reckoned a reign of thirteen months three years. He also corrects the next clause, which is not within that time but at that time, meaning at that crisis. Keil and Delitzsch go to the close, where Jephthah, having urged everything that could be pleaded — possession, length of time, right of conquest and undisputed occupation — leaves it to Jehovah the Judge to decide between the nations by giving the victory to the juster cause. Clarke reads that submission generously: if you be right and we wrong, the incorruptible Judge shall determine in your favour.
29:
The Spirit comes on him at the moment the argument fails. Gill glosses it from the Targum as the spirit of strength, a fortitude and courage and zeal such as was given to men when God raised them up to deliver Israel; and he sees in it a change of office, since Jephthah had been chosen general by the eastern tribes but was now qualified by God as judge of all Israel. Clarke reads it as a testimony rather than an equipment, God qualifying him for the work and so declaring his cause good. Henry has it come at the right moment in the story: only when the people's unanimous choice had shown he had a clear call, and the king of Ammon's obstinate deafness had shown he had a just cause, did the Spirit come upon him and advance his natural faculties, making him bolder and wiser than he had been. Henry even reads the route as evidence of it, thinking the choice of the way an instance of the discretion the Spirit gave, since those who walk after the Spirit are led forth the right way. Keil and Delitzsch make the march plainer: he passed through Gilead and Manasseh to raise an army, brought it to Mizpeh of Gilead where Israel was already encamped, and went on against the Ammonites, the verb in the last clause carrying a hostile sense. Ellicott would render it went through rather than passed over, since the object was to collect levies and rouse the tribes, and quotes the description of him sweeping through the land from end to end to kindle the torch of war.

Then, on the edge of the battle, he vows. Ellicott notes that vowing was a practice of all ancient nations and particularly of the Jews. Gill supposes he made it before setting out, hoping such a temper of mind would be acceptable and bring him success. Keil and Delitzsch quote the terms exactly — that whoever comes out of the doors of his house to meet him on his safe return shall belong to the Lord, and he will offer him for a burnt offering — and then close off one way of softening them. Whatever Jephthah had in mind, he cannot have meant a head of cattle or a beast of his flock, since the phrase about coming out of the doors of the house to meet a man will not describe a herd driven from the stall at the moment of his return, nor an animal that happens to run out; in every other place the phrase is used of people. Henry is more interested in what the vow reveals about the man who made it. There may be remainders of distrust even in the hearts of true and great believers, and Jephthah, who had every reason for confidence and the Spirit of the Lord besides, still hesitates when it comes to the settling and says if thou wilt without fail deliver them. Henry suspects the snare the vow brought him into was meant to correct that weakness, and the fond conceit that he could not count on victory unless he offered God something considerable in exchange for it. He is careful not to condemn vowing itself, which is good when we are in pursuit of a mercy, provided it is made as an expression of gratitude and not as a purchase of the favour, and provided the thing vowed tends to God's glory or to our own furtherance in his service.
31:
Everything turns on one word and one letter. Gill states the fork plainly: if to meet me is meant of intention, none but a human creature can be intended, since nothing else could come out by design; if it means only what happened to meet him, any creature may be. Clarke takes the second road and goes far down it. He would render the clause I will consecrate it to the Lord, or I will offer it for a burnt offering, and holds that such conditions must have been implied, since without them the vow would be that of a heathen or a madman — a dog could not be made a burnt offering, and a neighbour's child was not his to give. He presses the character of the man: Jephthah was deeply pious and well acquainted with the law, as his argument with Ammon shows, and could not commit the crime he had just been God's executioner to punish in others. He offers a conjecture too, that a single letter lost into the one beside it turned I will offer Him a burnt offering into I will offer it up for a burnt offering; and though the emendation is not strictly needed, he notes the Hebrew lacks the preposition it would normally carry for a burnt offering. His conclusion comes from the end of the chapter, where the daughter is said to have known no man: she was not sacrificed but consecrated to perpetual virginity.

Ellicott meets each argument and rejects them all. The rendering, he says, is certainly whosoever and not whatsoever, as the Greek and the Vulgate have it, and the marginal or for and comes of the same wish to soften the verse — an attempt, following the old Jewish commentators, to explain the plain meaning away out of deference to modern feeling. The animal reading he calls a notion Augustine himself ridiculed, and adds a practical objection: a single beast would be a strangely inadequate return, and quotes the question what sort of vow it would be for a prince to promise God the first calf that met him. He supposes Jephthah left God to choose the victim and probably expected a slave. Nor will Ellicott allow that such a thought was impossible for an Israelite. Human sacrifice was all but universal in the ancient world, particularly among the Syrians he had lived among and the Phoenicians whose gods Israel had lately taken up, and it was the special worship of the very nations he was marching against; the Law forbidding it was one thing and the observance of it quite another, as the Moloch-worship of the wilderness and of the later kings alike show.

The hardest of Clarke's points is the Spirit, and Ellicott answers it directly. To argue that a man on whom the Spirit had come could not have made so rash and evil a vow is to substitute idle fancies for clear facts. The Spirit clothed Gideon, and Gideon set up an illegal worship; the Spirit came upon Saul, and Saul was ready to kill his own son over a vow no less foolish than this one; the Spirit came upon David from the day of his anointing, and David sank into adultery and murder. The phrase, he concludes, is not a certificate of lasting spiritual attainment but a grant of divine strength for a particular end. What neither writer disputes is that Jephthah understood himself to be bound. Gill, who leaves the victim open, still fixes the terms narrowly, taking the vow to fall on whatever came out first, as the Latin has it, since at such a moment many might come out at once. Keil and Delitzsch, having already shut off the reading that makes it a beast of the flock, pass straight from the vow to the battle, where the Lord delivered the Ammonites into his hand.
32:
Ellicott is careful about the join. The word that opens the account of the battle is simply and, not so, and does not connect the victory to the vow at all but merely resumes the narrative. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott between them fix the ground: from Aroer to Minnith, which the old gazetteers put four miles from Heshbon, and on to Abel of the vineyards, which our version turns into the plain of the vineyards. Clarke reads the twenty cities as either taken or destroyed, with the whole Ammonite army routed. Gill notes that Jephthah came back to Mizpeh, where he had spoken his terms before the Lord and where he had settled such family as he had brought with him out of Tob. What met him there was a custom, not an accident: Clarke and Ellicott both note that women went out to meet returning conquerors with music and dancing, as Miriam met Moses and as the women of all the cities of Israel met Saul and David. Ellicott observes that the narrator adds she was his only child because he feels the pathos of it, and that the word he uses for only is a peculiarly tender one.

The father's cry is read closely. Ellicott renders the middle clause literally as crushing, thou hast crushed me, and explains why there was no way out. A vow was binding only when spoken, and the Hebrews knew two kinds — the simple vow that could be redeemed, and the ban, which was irredeemable and made the thing devoted a holy of holies to God. Jephthah, he says, treated his as a ban, and it never once occurred to him to escape the loss by treating it as the lesser kind; the Hebrews felt the awfulness of an oath too intensely to leave room for such reservations, as Saul showed when he was ready to kill his own son. Clarke reads the grief differently, taking Jephthah to be crushed because his only child would now leave his family extinct in Israel. Gill notices the small word our translators inserted: the daughter does not say if thou hast opened thy mouth, since the father had plainly told her what he had vowed, and Ellicott adds that the needless if a little weakens the heroism of her answer.

Her reply is what the commentators most admire. Clarke calls her at once obedient, pious and patriotic, and notes what her consent cost: to have no offspring was the utmost degradation among the Hebrews, and she was regardless of it, seeing her father safe and her country delivered. Ellicott will not defend the father's theology — he quotes Josephus, that the sacrifice was neither lawful nor acceptable to God — but he will praise the two of them for what remains, the faithfulness that would not go back from a vow though it were to his own hurt and the devotion of a daughter acquiescing in her own death for her country. He gathers the classical parallels around her, Iphigenia and Macaria and the Decii, and quotes the poets who have taken the same view of her. On her one request the commentators are agreed that nothing forbade the delay. Ellicott explains what she went to bewail, since the grief of a Hebrew maiden was not death but dying unwedded and childless, which cut off from her house the hopes that prophecy had cherished; he notes that Josephus softens it to bewailing her youth. Clarke, who reads the whole story as ending in consecration rather than death, takes her going up and down the mountains to mean no more than paying a farewell visit to each of her companions at home, which might well fill two months.
40:
The closing verse turns on a single verb, and none of them thinks our version has caught it. Clarke says flatly that to lament is not a correct translation, and gives a Latin rendering of the whole sentence in which the virgins of Israel go four days a year not to mourn Jephthah's daughter but to comfort her. Gill lays out the choices without deciding: some take it of lamenting her death and some of her virginity, but the word may equally mean to talk with her and hold conversation, which is how two of the rabbis understood it — the daughters bringing her news and diverting stories to cheer her in her solitude. He adds a third possibility from the Arabic, where the root means to praise, and notes that the same book uses it that way of rehearsing the righteous acts of the Lord; on that reading the yearly visit was to celebrate her heroism in submitting to her father's vow, and was paid to her in person and while she lived, to keep up her spirits. Ellicott reports the same sense from another rabbi and compares what the Romans felt for Claelia, or any nation for a heroine whose self-sacrifice bought it a victory.

Clarke uses the verse as evidence and then builds his whole case on it. If the custom was to comfort her, she was alive to be comforted, and he observes besides that nothing suggests the practice outlived her. He then sets out at length the exposition he follows, which turns the vow into two vows by reading the Hebrew conjunction disjunctively — whatever person met him should be the Lord's, or whatever clean beast met him should be a burnt offering. The idiom is defended from a parallel where the same particle must be read as or, since the paucity of connecting particles in Hebrew often forces that sense. The Levitical law of vows is then brought in to support it. A simple vow could be redeemed at a fixed price if a man repented of it, which the argument calls a wise provision against rash vows; but a vow of devotement was irredeemable, and the law naming it lists three subjects for three different uses — the man dedicated to God's service, as Samuel was by his mother; clean cattle to be sacrificed, and unclean ones set to carry burdens for the tabernacle; and land to be held as sacred property.

On that reading Jephthah's daughter falls under the first head. She was devoted irredeemably, and could not be bought back, but what she was devoted to was perpetual virginity in the service of the tabernacle, with her own consent; and Clarke notes that such service was already customary, since of the captive virgins taken in the Midianite war a tribute of thirty-two persons had gone to the Lord. He then turns the emotional difficulties of the story into arguments for his reading rather than against it. The father's extreme grief is perfectly natural in a man with no other child, who could now look forward only to the extinction of his name; and the daughter's request for two months is natural too, since childlessness was a reproach to women everywhere and peculiarly so in Israel, so that what she gave up generously she might still regret — the hope of becoming a mother in Israel. Whether the four days were kept in her memory or in her company is left standing as the last unsettled question of the chapter, and it is the same question as the vow itself, answered one way by those who read the verb as lamenting and another by those who read it as praise.
